header.tagline: Exploring reason through computation, painting grace one stroke at a time
header.introLine2: I draw, design, and write code—always taking on new projects and slowly working through the backlog. I love near-future and sci-fi works, as well as retro things, especially mechanical calculators and neon signs. I’m a former member of justfont and contributed to the Huninn typeface and open-source font projects. I also enjoy doujin events and cosplay.

design.title: Design
design.description: I like human-centered design that balances function and beauty. I contributed to justfont’s Huninn typeface and have also worked on graphic and web design.

drawing.title: Drawing
drawing.description: I love drawing and occasional doodling—especially maid outfits, glasses, sailor uniforms, animal ears, bunny girls, and competitive swimsuits!

photo.title: Photography
photo.description: I like using a camera to preserve things that only exist in a particular instant. I shoot Fujifilm, and lately I mainly shoot film.

model.description: I’m fascinated by the power and beauty condensed into tiny scales. I even have an airbrush at home for painting! I love building small things like ship models, planes, and miniature instruments.

doujin.description: I regularly attend FF, CWT, Comiket, and the like, and I set up a booth when I can. I love joining these events and chatting with everyone.

cosplay.description: I love cosplay and I’m still sharpening my makeup skills. I don’t handle heat well, so I usually cosplay at winter events. Let’s chat!

travel.title: Travel

opensource.title: Open source
opensource.description: I love writing code, and I also love sharing what I’ve learned and connecting with people. You’ll often spot me at open-source conferences such as COSCUP!

electronics.title: Electronics

nowPlaying.title: What I’m exploring lately

kumikoPage.architecture: Architecture shaped by the user experience

Edits are stored in browser IndexedDB and survive being offline or closing the tab.

splitFlapPage.hero: A React component that recreates station and airport split-flap displays. Pure CSS transform animations keep hundreds of flaps turning smoothly at once.
splitFlapPage.ideaText: Keikyu Kawasaki’s split-flap departure board retired in 2022, but the sound and rhythm of its mechanical motion remain captivating. react-split-flap recreates that feeling with CSS transforms: SplitFlap turns a string one character at a time, while LongFlap can turn an entire ReactNode—an image, icon, or a full layout—as one panel.
splitFlapPage.playgroundDescription: Type a few characters and watch each flap turn toward its target character.
splitFlapPage.inputLabel: Text shown on the split-flap display
splitFlapPage.clockText: A live clock that turns once per second. When the tab is in the background, its animation clock falls back to a coarse timer; it still shows the correct time when the tab returns to the foreground.

engineering.title: Shared animation clock
engineering.description: Every flap subscribes to one requestAnimationFrame loop. Turns that expire in the same frame are merged into a single React commit, so hundreds of simultaneous flaps render only once.

engineering.title: No DOM reconstruction
engineering.description: Flaps remain mounted without changing keys, alternating between two CSS animation names to start directly from the first frame. There is no per-flap Web Animations API read/write cycle.

engineering.title: Minimal compositing layers
engineering.description: Only the moving top and bottom halves are promoted to GPU layers. In a scene of about 400 flaps, this cuts compositing layers by about 70% and GPU time by about 27%.

zipcodePage.eyebrow: Paste the whole address and be done
zipcodePage.hero: Look up Taiwan ZIP codes from addresses that were never split into fields, and render them in English following Chunghwa Post's own rules. It understands 台/臺, full-width characters, and Chinese numerals, and works even without the city or district — every lookup runs client-side, with no server, WASM, or SQLite.

notes: A full address resolves to six digits, carried into the English form.
台 is normalized to 臺, and Zhongzheng Dist. is filled in.
The road name is unique, so Zhongshan Dist., Taipei is filled in.
P.O. boxes use a separate post-office table.
Falls back to three digits, with the city still filled in.

zipcodePage.idea: Addresses as users actually paste them
zipcodePage.ideaText: Addresses in a form are rarely split cleanly: raw strings pasted by users, OCR output, and single text columns inherited from older systems all arrive as one run of text. tw-address-tools takes them as-is, with no requirement to separate city, district, and road first. It is a JavaScript port of the matching algorithm in moskytw/zipcodetw, with no runtime dependencies.
zipcodePage.fuzzyText: It first normalizes 台/臺, full-width characters, and common Chinese numerals, then splits the address into city, district, road section, lane, alley, and house-number fragments and matches them layer by layer. With enough information it applies the house-number rules and returns six digits; with less, it falls back to a usable three-digit code — and when the address is ambiguous it returns an empty string rather than guessing.
fuzzyNotes: A complete address matches the house-number rules and returns six digits.
台 is normalized to 臺; a road name alone is enough.
A district on its own returns a usable three-digit code.
The road name is unique nationwide, so the city and district are filled back in.
zipcodePage.unique: The missing parts, filled back in
zipcodePage.uniqueText: When an address omits the city or district, and what remains matches exactly one road in Taiwan, the missing fragments are restored and matching continues to six digits. If several roads match — Zhongzheng Rd. exists nearly everywhere — the address is left alone rather than guessed.
zipcodePage.speedText: The browser index flattens sorted data into one string per column with Int32Array offsets and binary search: about a quarter of the memory, still around 500,000 lookups per second.
metrics: Loading the index in a browser
zipcodePage.speedFootnote: Measured against Chunghwa Post's June 2026 3+3 ZIP code data — 79,845 house-number rules and 162,470 gradual address entries — on an Apple M3 Pro. A 90,950-query differential test against the Python reference implementation reports zero differences.
zipcodePage.mailboxText: A box address is not a street address: its ZIP code comes straight from the post office's name, never from the house-number rules. 899 post offices that actually operate boxes are covered; the source data lists another 314 that have six-digit codes assigned but no box service yet, and those always return an empty string — the number looks deliverable but is not.
zipcodePage.openSource: MIT licensed, open source, free to use
zipcodePage.openSourceText: What ships is the source: no build step, loadable directly in a browser. TypeScript declarations are included for both the Node and browser entry points, so no @types package is needed. The data comes as three independent dictionaries — the address index, the P.O. box table, and the Chinese-English name tables — so you load only the ones you need.
zipcodePage.credit: The ZIP code directory, Chinese-English name tables, and P.O. box data all come from Chunghwa Post, used under its 3+3 ZIP code open licensing statement and the Open Government Data License. The matching algorithm is ported from moskytw/zipcodetw.
zipcodePage.translate: English addresses, while we are at it
zipcodePage.translateText: translate() reverses the word order and inserts the ZIP code following Chunghwa Post's own writing rules, producing an English address you can print straight onto an envelope. Every name comes from the official Chinese-English tables — nothing is romanized by guesswork — and against the bundled directory, 99.99% of addresses translate completely.
translateNotes: Floor, number, alley, lane, and section each map to the official abbreviation, with the ZIP code looked up and inserted.
English post-office names for P.O. boxes also come from official data; the fields become the box number and the office name.

Siwei 3rd Rd. is in Lingya Dist., Kaohsiung — Xinyi Dist. has no such road. A name being translatable does not make the address real, so cross-validation returns an empty string rather than an English address that cannot be delivered.
zipcodePage.usageText: No runtime dependencies, and what ships is the source. On Node you import and query directly; browsers have no fs, so loadZipcode() fetches the data files published with the package. TypeScript declarations are bundled, so no @types package is needed.

api.title: Common API
rows: Returns a directly usable three- or six-digit ZIP code, or an empty string when nothing is certain — never an invalid four- or five-digit intermediate prefix.
Use it when the UI needs to show how the address matched: returns { zipcode, source, resolution }, or null when nothing is found.
Sub-functions that search only street addresses or only P.O. boxes, for when the data is guaranteed to be one form.
Returns { english, parts, untranslated, complete }. The ZIP code is looked up and inserted automatically, or supplied via { zipcode }.
Loads the data files in a browser and builds a Zipcode whose methods share the names above. The three dictionaries are independent — load only what you need.
The Chinese-English tables for browsers; wire up verify and mailbox for road cross-validation and P.O. box translation.

features.title: The familiar way, made easier
features.description: Careful refinements preserve the familiar feel while improving security and performance.

items.title: Adaptive candidates
items.description: The input method looks at the sentence and your selection history when ordering candidates. Characters you choose often rise to the top next time.

items.title: Add phrases
items.description: Hold Shift and press ← to expand the selection one character at a time, then press Enter to add it to your user dictionary. Ctrl+3 adds the three characters before the cursor directly (Ctrl+1–9 sets the length).

items.title: Symbol table
items.description: Control+Command+. opens the symbol table. When the composition area is empty, Ctrl+0 also shows punctuation candidates.

items.title: Traditional-to-Simplified Chinese
items.description: Control+Command+G toggles the output filter: type Bopomofo as usual and commit Simplified Chinese. Command+Shift+Space toggles full-width Latin characters.

items.title: Tab segmentation
items.description: Move the cursor to where you want a break while composing and press Tab to force segmentation—the sentence is then recomposed around that boundary.

items.title: The old friends are still here
items.description: The default is smart Bopomofo composition, while the traditional Bopomofo, Cangjie, and Simple modules from the OpenVanilla era remain available. You can also import your own .cin tables to add table-based methods such as Cantonese or Hakka.

history.title: What is ChiaKey?
history.description: ChiaKey is a macOS input method for Traditional Chinese that uses Bopomofo (also known as Zhuyin), the phonetic script commonly used in Taiwan. Built from Yahoo! KeyKey’s open-source code, it carries its familiar experience forward while continually repairing, improving, and building a new lexicon and language model.
history.body: After ending the project, Yahoo! released its code as open source. ChiaKey starts from that codebase: replacing obsolete APIs, repairing missing pieces, and continually improving the app, its performance, and its lexicon so the familiar input experience can keep evolving on modern macOS.

timeline.title: Yahoo! KeyKey launches
timeline.description: A free, cross-platform intelligent input method.

timeline.title: Project closes; source code opens
timeline.description: Released under a BSD-style license on GitHub (YahooArchive/KeyKey). The final installer has been continuously adapted by the community ever since.

timeline.title: Apple announces the end of x86 support
timeline.description: The final-generation installer will no longer install on macOS 26 and later.

timeline.title: ChiaKey
timeline.description: Repairs the app and keeps building its word-selection lexicon for Apple Silicon and modern macOS.

principles.title: Keep the familiar feel
principles.description: The first goal is to carry forward Yahoo! KeyKey’s composition and candidate window, while a new lexicon makes that familiar feel better suited to Taiwanese usage today.

principles.title: Modernize carefully
principles.description: Improve security and algorithms with modern APIs and compile for Apple Silicon.

principles.title: A conservative pace
principles.description: ChiaKey is not trying to compete on features with modern input methods. Its focus is stability.

lexicon.title: Layered lexicons that understand you
lexicon.description: A lexicon is more than one list. ChiaKey combines multiple sources to preserve a familiar feel while continuously choosing vocabulary suited to everyday Taiwanese usage; after installation on your Mac, it adds two layers that are yours.

layers.title: Everyday word data
layers.description: Combines everyday characters, words, and readings so you can type daily Chinese smoothly.

layers.title: Context-aware corrections
layers.description: When words sound alike, it refers to the surrounding context to help choose the candidate that best fits the sentence.

layers.title: Recently trending words
layers.description: Automatically collects trending topics and names from the web, then updates the lexicon.

layers.title: Taiwan usage adjustments
layers.description: Adjusts common Taiwanese writing and candidate order, while reducing words being split or combined incorrectly.

layers.title: User dictionary + learning cache
layers.description: The words you add and your selection habits stay on this Mac; custom words can be imported or exported.

highlights.intro: The lexicon was the hardest part of this project.

items.title: 470 million characters for more accurate selection
items.body: Yahoo! KeyKey used surrounding words to help choose characters, but that data was never released with its code. ChiaKey draws on about 470 million characters of real Taiwanese text—government news, Legislative Yuan transcripts, PTT, Plurk, and Traditional Chinese Wikipedia—to find word pairings that help distinguish homophones in context.

items.title: Trending words, freshly stocked
items.body: Language evolves over time. ChiaKey tries to keep up by regularly watching for trending words and loading them automatically with every lexicon update. It carries forward more than the code: the lexicon keeps moving forward too.

update.title: Update lexicons without reinstalling
update.before: The built-in word data is independently updated after
update.after: builds ChiaKey-Lexicon. The input method automatically checks the newest version before enabling it. Your custom phrases and selection history stay on your Mac.

download.title: Install
download.description: Download and install the .pkg, then add ChiaKey in System Settings → Keyboard → Input Sources. Apple Silicon is supported.
download.disclaimer: ChiaKey is not an official Yahoo product. Its source is released under a BSD-style license; the Yahoo! name and contributor names may not endorse derivative products without written permission.

items.q: How is ChiaKey related to Yahoo! KeyKey?
items.a: ChiaKey starts from the code Yahoo! open-sourced after KeyKey was discontinued. It carries the familiar input experience forward while extensively repairing and improving it, building a new lexicon and language model, and maintaining compatibility wherever possible. It is not an official Yahoo product; the source is released under a BSD-style license.

items.q: Why can’t Yahoo! KeyKey continue to run on new Macs?
items.a: The last official installer is Intel-only and needs Rosetta on Apple Silicon. Apple has announced that macOS 26 and later will no longer support Intel architecture. ChiaKey runs natively on Apple Silicon and modern macOS.

items.q: Can older Intel Macs use ChiaKey?
items.a: Yes. The current minimum deployment target is macOS 10.13 High Sierra, which almost every Intel Mac from 2009 onward can upgrade to.
Yes—free and open source. Download the .pkg to install; the source code is on GitHub.

items.q: Can I import my Yahoo! KeyKey dictionary?
items.a: ChiaKey is fully compatible with Yahoo! KeyKey dictionaries, including data accumulated through smart learning. Go to Preferences → Phrase Management → Import Yahoo Input Method Data. Note: because of KeyKey’s architecture, Yahoo! KeyKey must be running to use this import.

items.q: Can I add plug-in input methods, such as Cantonese or Taiwanese?
items.a: Yes. Older .cin table input methods can be imported. ChiaKey keeps OpenVanilla’s table engine: in Preferences → Custom Input Methods, click + or drag a .cin table file onto the list. It will then appear in the input menu. Tables for Cantonese, Hakka, Taiwanese, Array, Dayi and more are available from projects such as cin-tables.

items.q: I love this project! How can I support it?
items.a: Thank you! You can support the project through <koFi>Ko-fi.com</koFi> (outside Taiwan) or <ecpay>ECPay sponsorship</ecpay> (Taiwan credit cards, Apple Pay, ATM, or convenience-store payment codes only).

items.q: A candidate looks wrong or a word is missing—how can I report it?
items.a: Please use the <report>GitHub report page</report> to report a missing word or candidate issue.

terminalPage.title: Talk to Akitsune
terminalPage.intro: A response terminal left behind in the shrine office. It is not connected to any language model — just the ChiaKey input method dictionary and a hand-written rule table. It segments what you type into words, then matches the closest rule. Fast to answer, and easy to catch out. Note: she only understands Chinese.
terminalPage.lexiconEmpty: What you type gets cut into words here first, then matched against the rules.
terminalPage.how1: Segmentation runs on data from the ChiaKey Lexicon: the NAER word frequency table, the libchewing dictionary, and a modern layer drawn from Taiwanese web corpora — about 70,000 entries. The browser solves the maximum-probability path, the same principle the input method uses to pick characters.
terminalPage.how2: Replies come from a hand-written rule table. Regex patterns first; if nothing matches, keyword overlap is scored against the segmented tokens. If that also misses, she picks the most meaningful word in your sentence and asks about it — the ELIZA move.
terminalPage.how3: LINK in the bottom left tracks whether the conversation is landing. It rises when she has an answer and falls when she does not; at the bottom the line starts breaking up. The whole page is under 300 KB.
